# Breaking Perfection: How the Giants' relentless rush shattered New England's dynasty

**By Steve Wyche**
**CNN Sports**

**GLENDALE, Arizona (CNN)** -- For 18 consecutive games, the New England Patriots’ offensive line operated like a pristine, impenetrable fortress. They protected the NFL’s MVP, paved the way for a record-shattering 589 points, and rendered Tom Brady virtually untouchable. 

Then came Super Bowl XLII. 

In a 17-14 shocker on Sunday night at University of Phoenix Stadium that will echo through NFL history, the New York Giants didn’t just defeat the undefeated Patriots—they physically dismantled them. The blueprint for ruining New England’s bid for a 19-0 season wasn't hidden in a complex playbook; it was executed on the line of scrimmage by a furious, four-man pass rush that left Brady bruised, battered, and out of answers.

"They played a great game," a visibly sore Brady said after the loss, his left knee wrapped and his face marked by the game's physical toll. "I’m certainly feeling it today. They came after us, they disrupted our timing, and we just couldn't get into any kind of rhythm. You give credit to their front—they made the plays when they had to, and we didn't."

The numbers tell part of the story: five sacks, 12 official quarterback hits, and dozens of forced rushes. But the true story was the relentless nature of Giants defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s rotation. 

By relying almost exclusively on his front four—defensive ends Michael Strahan, Osi Umenyiora, and Justin Tuck, along with defensive tackles Barry Cofield and Fred Robbins—Spagnuolo unlocked the holy grail of modern defense. The Giants managed to generate suffocating, immediate pressure while dropping seven defenders into coverage, effectively eliminating Brady’s quick passing lanes.

"They outplayed us up front, plain and simple," said Patriots head coach Bill Belichick, whose team was held to its lowest point total of the season. "They got pressure with four guys, and when a team can do that and drop seven into coverage, it makes it tough on any offense. We didn't do a good enough job protecting, and we didn't do a good enough job making adjustments."

The key to the Giants' scheme was versatility, particularly the play of Tuck. Spagnuolo frequently employed his "NASCAR" package, moving Tuck inside to defensive tackle alongside rookie Jay Alford, flanked by Strahan and Umenyiora on the edges. The speed proved overwhelming for New England’s interior offensive line. Center Dan Koppen and guards Logan Mankins and Stephen Neal—accustomed to anchoring against power—were repeatedly beaten by Tuck’s quickness off the ball. 

Tuck finished with two sacks and a forced fumble, but his constant push up the middle prevented Brady from stepping up in the pocket to throw long.

For Patriots wide receiver Randy Moss, who caught what seemed to be the game-winning touchdown late in the fourth quarter before Eli Manning's miracle drive, the loss was a nightmare end to a historic campaign. 

"To come this far and fall short, it hurts. It’s a hurt that is going to stay for a long time," Moss said in a quiet New England locker room. "Their front four played a hell of a game. They kept Tom off balance, they hit him, and they didn't let us take the shots downfield that got us here. You have to tip your hat to them. They beat us."

When Brady finally did escape the rush on the Patriots' final drive, needing a field goal to tie, the Giants' front line provided the exclamation point. On second-and-10 with less than 20 seconds remaining, rookie Jay Alford burst through a collapsing pocket and slammed Brady to the turf for a 10-yard loss, effectively sealing the biggest upset in Super Bowl history.

Strahan, the 36-year-old veteran who contemplated retirement last summer, summed up the defensive line’s mindset after celebrating under a cloud of blue and red confetti.

"We knew if we gave Tom time, he’d pick us apart. He’s the best," Strahan said. "So we made a pact. We said, 'It's on us. It's on the front four.' We didn't need to blitz. We just needed to hunt."

They hunted, they conquered, and in doing so, the Giants' pass rush didn't just win a Lombardi Trophy—it broke perfection.
